sources.note: Nothing. The report treats 'Lohari-Lahul' (the smiths' language spoken throughout Lahul, c. 150 speakers per Census 2001) only as a name/area/number/classification entry: it places Chinuli, Lohari-Lahul and Tindiyali under Grierson's Western Pahari group of Indo-Aryan (p. 3), states verbatim 'Spitian, Lohari-Lahul, Miyari and Tindiyali have not been studied. Therefore no individual distinctive feature about any of them can be given.' (p. 4), and adds that 'Lohari-Lahuli is closely related to' Chinali as studied by D.D. Sharma 1991 (p. 4). No phonology, no remark on tone, accent or stress for…

sources.citation: Tobdan (ed.). 2010. Kunzom [कुन्जोम], varsh 4, ank 5-6 (January-December 2009 & 2010). Annual magazine of the language and culture of Lahaul & Spiti. Kullu/Keylong: Society for Conservation & Promotion of Culture in Lahaul & Spiti. In Hindi and local languages. Lohari ('लोहार भाषा / लोहार बोली') items: 'गरीब मठा' (Lohar-bhasha rendering of the Hindi story 'नालायक बेटा', by Dr Randhir Singh Manepa); 'खरगोश, ब्राग: की कथा' (story, by Karma); 'पहेली, लोहार भाषा' (riddle, by Kerma). archive.org item kunzom-vol-04-2010 (scan + Hindi scanned text).
sources.note: No phonology content. Three connected Lohari prose texts (c. 2.5 printed pages) and one riddle in plain Devanagari orthography, no tone/stress/length marking, no grammatical or phonological commentary; editorial and articles say nothing about Lohari structure. First published running text in Lahul Lohar (primary data), not a description.

sources.citation: Sharma, D.D. (Devidatta Sarma). 1991. A Descriptive Grammar & Vocabulary of Chinali. Shimla: Himachal Academy of Arts, Culture and Languages. 74 pp. (archive.org IIAS-85180, open, text)
sources.note: Phonology chapter concerns Chinali only. Lohari appears only in the Introduction: sec. 0.2 (p. 1) Chinali is 'quite unintelligible to the members of any other community, except the Gara or Lohar community which speaks a variety of Indo-Aryan'; sec. 0.4 (p. 1) 'the data for Lohari was recorded from Shri Ram Singh of Shansha'. No Lohari description, sound system or vocabulary anywhere in the book (a full-text search for stress/accent: only these two hits). Nothing on Lohari stress.

sources.citation: Sharma, D.D. 1989. Tribal Languages of Himachal Pradesh, Part I (Studies in Tibeto-Himalayan Languages II). Delhi: Mittal Publications. (archive.org CL-CSKHPKV-15657, scanned text)

General Introduction pp. 6-7: Chinali (Dagi) and Lohari are Indo-Aryan dialects of the Chahn and Lohar communities, discovered by the author in 1980; 'Chinali shows a higher degree of preservation of Old Indo-Aryan elements as compared with Lohari'; p. 12: 'The historical relationship of Chinali/Lohari has been taken up separately, along with their description' (only the Chinali description, Sharma 1991, is known to have appeared).
